rv.q: In the midst of the busy fall theater season, Classic Stage Company’s triumphant Off-Broadway revival of the underrated 2002 chamber musical “A Man of No Importance,” starring Jim Parsons and directed by John Doyle, comes as a most welcome and most unexpected surprise.
This revival — the first since its New York premiere in 2002 — has songs and performances that will rouse the soul, and that's of the utmost importance.
Whatever the ups and downs of his work in years past, A Man of No Importance is a definite highlight in his tenure, and a great way to say goodbye.
A Man of No Importance is an example, at best a mildly pleasant, mildly moving pastime well below the standards Flaherty, Ahrens, and McNally set for themselves (with Drabinsky prodding?).
But Doyle’s production remains oddly lifeless — and even moments of violence pass by without so much as a blip to raise the blood pressure.
His is an indolent, entitled performance.
In that space, the charm and energy of this show just can't be denied.
Still, the performances and score of A Man of No Importance lift it up, and Doyle’s production, his last as artistic director of Classic Stage Company, is on the whole a pleasure.
Revived by the Classic Stage Company and presented in its intimate space, the play takes on a warmth and closeness.
The reality is the disconnect exists and the production suffers as a result.

cn.t: Jim Parsons leads a heartfelt revival of this underrated chamber musical that critics find touching and well-intentioned, though some fault his performance and the production's modest impact.
